docs.title: How the heat outlook is made
docs.what.p: Every morning the outlook collects the forecast runs of three families of global weather models for the next seven days: GFS from the United States, ICON from Germany and GEM from Canada. Each run is a slightly different but plausible version of the coming days. Together they show what is most likely and how sure we can be.
docs.correct.p: Global models are often a little too warm or too cool at one place. Every day the forecasts are compared with what the city's weather station measured, and the average difference of recent weeks is removed, separately for each model family.
docs.levels.hi: In Kaolack and Khulna the levels are based on the heat index, how hot it feels once humidity is taken into account. Each city has its own levels, Caution, Danger, Extreme and Critical, set for its climate.
docs.levels.lima: In Lima heat becomes a risk when both the day and the night stay unusually warm for the time of year, as in SENAMHI's heat wave definition. A level starts where the station's own record counts a day or a night as unusual for that date, and never below a fixed minimum for each level.
docs.rule.h: When a day gets a level
docs.rule.p: A day gets a level when at least 30 in 100 forecasts reach it, with each model family counting equally. The chance shown for each level is that share. In Lima, Danger and Extreme also need two of the three model families to agree.
docs.range.p: Eight in ten forecasts fall inside the likely range. The number on each day card is the middle forecast, the most likely value.
docs.later.h: Why later days are less certain
docs.later.p: The further ahead, the more the forecasts drift apart and the more often they miss. The first days are for acting, the later days for planning. Email alerts cover the first three days only, and the track record shows how well each lead time has done.
docs.official.p: The national weather services issue the official warnings: ANACIM in Senegal, BMD in Bangladesh and SENAMHI in Peru. When one is in force, the page shows it first. This outlook is local and experimental, and it can differ from a warning for a wider area. Follow the official warning.
docs.track.h: How the track record is scored
docs.track.p: Each forecast is compared with the measurement at the city's station once it is in. A hit is a day forecast at Danger or higher that was measured at Danger or higher. A miss is a day measured at Danger or higher that was forecast lower. A false alarm is a day forecast at Danger or higher that was measured lower.
docs.data.p: Each city's outlook is a public data file, updated every morning. It holds the seven days with their levels, chances and ranges, the official warning, and the verified history. Its format may still change, so please contact us before building on it.
docs.status.p: This outlook is a research forecast under test in Practical Action's Living in a Hotter World project, built by Meteory. It is not an official warning.
